newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM seen winning debate but surprises possible.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM seen winning debate but surprises possible.

text.p: Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa is likely to win a no-confidence vote against him in parliament but a surprise twist cannot be ruled out, political analysts said on Wednesday.

Given the fluidity of Thai politics, there is a chance that Banharn could surprise everyone by dissolving parliament before the crucial vote is taken or might even quit and hand over his post to another coalition politician, they said.

Key opposition leaders lambasted Banharn when the debate opened in parliament on Wednesday, accusing him of condoning corruption in his administration and mismanaging the national economy. A vote will be taken after the debate, which is expected to last three days.

The opposition motion, aimed solely at Banharn, accuses him among other things of incompetence, economic mismanagement and plagiarism in his master's thesis. Barharn has denied all the accusations and vowed to defend himself in parliament.
Banharn, who leads a 14-month-old, six-party coalition, controls 209 of the 391 seats in parliament and on paper has the numbers to thwart the opposition, analysts said.
His administration has been plagued by intra-coalition squabbling and a slowdown in the traditionally robust economy.

Sluggish export growth this year, a battered stock market that dived to near three-year-lows last week, rumours of devaluation of the baht and a hostile local media have been other problems, analysts said.
Banharn's coalition partners have pledged to support him through the debate, although in recent weeks some have said that things could change after the vote.
"It depends on how much the opposition will bring out in terms of strong evidence against him," said Somchai Phagaphasvivat, political scientist at Thammasat University.
"If there is much negative public reaction to the accusations, some partners might withdraw support and Banharn may be forced to dissolve parliament before the vote," he told Reuters.
But Somchai said he believe that it was unlikely Banharn would dissolve parliament before the vote.

No Thai prime minister has ever been put out of office by a no-confidence vote in parliament, analysts noted. In the past, however, prime ministers have quit just before a vote or been toppled by the army.
Analysts said that, given past history, there was an outside chance that Banharn could step down before the vote is taken if he smelled defeat.
Others said that if Banharn survived the vote, surprises could still be in store.
If Banharn wins the vote, he could could choose to remain as premier and launch a major cabinet reshuffle to appease coalition partners.

"If he survives, I think there could be a major cabinet reshuffle," said Irene Tang of Paribas Capital Markets. Other economic analysts also expected the government to take firmer and decisive measures to tackle economic woes like a rising current account deficit and sagging exports.
However, there was no guarantee Banharn would remain for long as some outspoken coalition partners have said they might change their view on him after the debate.

Banharn could also step down some time after winning the vote, to let another coalition leader take his post, realign and strengthen his coalition by including other opposition parties or dissolving parliament to try to make a comeback.
Most of Banharn's coalition partners are against holding fresh elections. Their dilemma is how to change the prime minister without going for another election.
"If I were Banharn, I would not resign or hand power to other politicians. I would rather dissolve the house instead," said Jonchai Thiengtham, a political aide to Banharn.
